evidence.label: A torsion-free counterexample to reduced Baum–Connes injectivity
A torsion-free counterexample to the Kadison–Kaplansky projection conjecture
An irrational-trace counterexample to reduced Baum–Connes

headline: Claims torsion-free groups that break the Kadison–Kaplansky projection conjecture and reduced Baum–Connes.
scope: Coefficient-free reduced Baum–Connes assembly for countable discrete groups, and projections in reduced group C*-algebras of torsion-free groups.
plain: To each group one can attach an algebra of operators, the reduced group C*-algebra. Two famous conjectures predict what this algebra looks like for well-behaved groups. Three companion papers claim to build groups where these predictions fail. One group has no elements of finite order, yet its algebra holds a projection other than 0 and 1. Another group's algebra holds a projection whose trace is irrational, which the Baum–Connes conjecture forbids.
doesNot: This does not disprove the classical Novikov conjecture or maximal rational injectivity, and it gives no finitely presented example.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Paul Baum and Alain Connes, manuscript formulating the conjecture
scorecard.significanceWhy: Baum–Connes and Kadison–Kaplansky are central conjectures linking group geometry and operator algebras; counterexamples would reshape the field.

explanation:
Start with a group that has two elements, 1 and g, where g times g is 1. Build formal sums a·1 + b·g with complex numbers a and b. Now take e = (1 + g)/2. Squaring gives (1 + 2g + g²)/4 = (2 + 2g)/4, which is e again. An element equal to its own square is a projection. The trace of a sum is its coefficient on 1, so e has trace 1/2. This projection exists because g has finite order. An element of finite order other than 1 is called torsion.

Torsion-free groups seem to behave differently. Take the integers under addition. Their operator algebra turns out to be the continuous functions on a circle. A projection is then a function taking only the values 0 and 1. On a connected circle, such a function must be constant. So the only projections are 0 and 1.

The Kadison–Kaplansky conjecture says this holds for every torsion-free group. The algebra is the reduced group C*-algebra, the closure of the group's sums acting on square-summable sequences. Pimsner and Voiculescu proved the conjecture for free groups[7]. A main route to it is the Baum–Connes conjecture. That conjecture says an assembly map, from the group's topology to the algebra's K-theory, is an isomorphism[1]. K-theory sorts projections into classes. Baum and Connes circulated it in 1982 and published it in 2000[2]. It is known for large classes of groups, including all countable amenable groups[6]. Earlier counterexamples of Higson, Lafforgue and Skandalis used extra coefficients. They do not break the coefficient-free form[12]. The obstacle was to find a group, with no coefficients, whose algebra escapes the topology.

The three papers claim to do that. The first builds a finitely generated torsion-free group whose assembly map sends a class of infinite order to zero[3]. The group is finitely generated, but finite presentation is not part of the conclusion[5]. It disproves neither maximal rational injectivity nor the classical Novikov conjecture[4]. The second builds a finitely generated torsion-free group with a projection other than 0 and the identity[8]. Its trace lies strictly between 0 and 1/2. That projection is in the completed algebra, not in the group ring of finite sums[9]. The third uses Lück's theorem: every assembly class has a rational trace[10]. It then builds a finitely generated group with a projection of irrational trace[11]. That projection cannot come from assembly. The constructions use expander graphs, sparse networks that are still very well connected.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has not checked any part of it. Each claim rests on a long chain of graph, spectral and operator estimates. No specialist review of the papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Landmark if it holds: these are counterexamples to two central conjectures. There is no Lean check and no published specialist review, so the claims are unconfirmed.

glossary.meaning: A group in which no element other than the identity returns to the identity after finitely many repeats.
An element of an algebra equal to its own square and to its own adjoint, like e = (1 + g)/2 above.
Here, the coefficient on the identity element; for the example e it is 1/2.
The algebra of operators made by letting the group act on square-summable sequences and closing up in norm.
A way of sorting projections in an algebra into classes that can be added.
A map from topological data about the group to the K-theory of its reduced C*-algebra.
Every element is a product of finitely many fixed generators and their inverses.
A sparse network of points and links that is still very well connected.
